title: Why our reconciliation job stopped scaling at forty million rows
summary: A nightly job went from three hours to nine. The fix was not a bigger machine, it was moving the logic into the database.
body:
Every engineering team has a job that runs at night and that everyone is a little afraid of. Ours was the reconciliation job. It compared the bank's statement to our ledger, and for two years it finished before anyone got to the office.

Then it did not.

## The shape of the problem

The job loaded both sides into memory as maps keyed by transaction reference, walked one map, and looked up each entry in the other. That is linear, and linear is fine until your maps are forty million entries each and the process spends most of its time in garbage collection.

We tried the obvious things first:

- A bigger instance. It bought us three weeks.
- Batching the load. It made the code harder to read and saved twenty minutes.
- Running two workers. They fought over the same rows.

## What actually worked

We stopped treating the database as a place to fetch rows from and started treating it as the thing that does the matching.

```sql
INSERT INTO matches (ledger_id, bank_id, stage)
SELECT l.id, b.id, 'exact'
FROM ledger l
JOIN bank_staging b
  ON b.reference = l.reference
 AND b.amount = l.amount;
```

A single hash join over indexed columns matched ninety-seven percent of rows in about four minutes. The remaining three percent went through two more stages with progressively looser rules, and anything left over landed in an audit table with the reason it failed each stage.

## The part nobody talks about

The biggest win was not speed. Moving the rules into SQL meant the finance team could read them. They found two rules that had been wrong for a year. No amount of Go refactoring would have surfaced that.

title: Notes from shipping offline-first sync
summary: Lessons from building sync for people who are offline for a week at a time, and why I stopped showing them conflict dialogs.
body:
Fieldnotes users are offline for days. When they come back, three of them have edited the same site record. The first version of the app asked them to choose which edits to keep. Nobody could remember. Everyone picked the top option.

## Conflict dialogs are a design failure

A conflict dialog says: the software could not decide, so you must. But the user has less context than the software does. They do not remember what they typed on Tuesday. They just want their notes.

So the goal became: never show a dialog. Merge everything, deterministically, and make the merge rule simple enough that a surveyor could predict it.

## Per-field registers

Each note is a set of fields. Each field is a last-writer-wins register with a hybrid logical clock. Two people editing different fields never conflict. Two people editing the same field converge on the later write, and the earlier write is kept in a visible history so nothing is silently gone.

This is not fancy. It covers almost every real case, because surveyors rarely edit the same short field at the same time.

## The one field that needed more

The long-form description was different. Two people would each add a paragraph, and last-writer-wins would throw one away. That field is now a small sequence CRDT, and both paragraphs survive. It took a week and it was the only place the extra machinery paid for itself.

## Things I would tell past me

1. Start with the simplest merge rule and measure how often it is wrong.
2. Keep history visible. Users forgive a merge they can undo.
3. Sync does not need to be realtime to feel instant. A batch every few seconds is plenty.

title: A boring deployment pipeline is a feature
summary: We removed a queue, a cache and a container orchestrator from a system that did not need them. It got faster and nobody misses them.
body:
When I joined the Dispatch project, deploying meant: push to main, wait for a container build, wait for a rollout across a small Kubernetes cluster, then check three dashboards. It took twenty minutes and one person understood it.

## What we removed

- **The message queue.** It carried about forty messages a minute between two services that lived on the same machine. A function call did the same job.
- **The cache.** It hid a slow query. We fixed the query and the cache had nothing left to do.
- **The orchestrator.** Two small instances behind a load balancer handle the traffic with room to spare.

## What we kept

One Next.js application. One Postgres database. One Redis instance for live driver positions, because that is a workload Redis is genuinely good at.

Deploys are a single GitHub Actions job that runs the tests, builds, and restarts the service. It takes four minutes. Everyone on the team has done one.

## The argument

Every component you add is a component you have to understand at three in the morning. The bar for adding one should be high, and the bar for removing one should be low. Most systems I have seen would be better with fewer parts, not more.

title: What I learned reviewing three hundred pull requests
summary: Patterns from a year of code review: what actually catches bugs, what is just noise, and how to write a comment someone wants to read.
body:
Last year I kept a note every time a review comment of mine caught something that would have reached production. After three hundred pull requests, here is what the note says.

## What caught bugs

- Reading the tests first, then asking what they do not cover.
- Following every early return and asking what state the caller is left in.
- Checking what happens when a list is empty. It is empty more often than you think.

## What did not

- Style comments. The formatter should own those.
- Suggesting a different abstraction on a change that works. That is a separate conversation.
- Anything I wrote after the fortieth minute of a review session.

## Writing comments people want to read

Say what you see, why it matters, and what you would do. Three short sentences. Mark anything optional as optional. If you are asking a question, make sure it is a real one and not a suggestion wearing a question mark.

The best review comment I received all year was: *This works, and I think it will surprise the next person who reads it. Would a comment explaining the retry help?* It was right, it was kind, and it took ten seconds to act on.
